name: Kubernetes
tagline: Container orchestration to evaluate when teams need controlled deployment, scheduling and operations at scale.
description: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform to evaluate when workloads require coordinated deployment, scheduling, scaling and recovery. It adds operational complexity, so suitability depends on workload needs, team expertise, security and the managed service or cluster model selected.
pros: Declarative deployment and scheduling can support repeatable operations for suitable workloads.
Health checks and rollout controls can be tested against known failure cases.
A well-defined platform model can standardize deployment across services.
cons: Cluster operations, upgrades, networking and permissions require specialist ownership.
For simple workloads, orchestration may add more complexity than value.
Costs include engineering time and observability, not just cluster resources.

content.title: Decide whether orchestration is needed
content.body: List the operational problem that requires Kubernetes: service scheduling, deployment consistency, scaling, recovery or platform standardization. Compare the expected benefit with a simpler managed runtime. Do not adopt orchestration only because it is common in other organizations.

content.title: Deploy a representative service
content.body: Package one service, configure health checks, resource requests and limits, secrets, service discovery and rollout behavior. Test a bad image, failed readiness check and rollback. Verify that deployment status and logs are understandable to the on-call engineer.

content.title: Security and reliability
content.body: Review RBAC, service accounts, network policies, secrets, image provenance, patching and cluster access. Test what happens when a node or dependency fails. Define upgrade ownership and a recovery plan before running business-critical workloads.

content.title: Observability and cost
content.body: Measure resource requests versus actual use, logs, metrics, storage, network and control-plane costs. Alert on user-impacting symptoms rather than every low-level event. Include engineer time for upgrades, incident response and platform maintenance in the cost estimate.

content.title: Operational readiness
content.body: Document cluster ownership, supported versions, backup and restore, capacity planning, deployment approvals and incident escalation. Start with a limited workload and prove the operating model before migrating additional services.

faqs.question: Who should evaluate Kubernetes?
faqs.answer: Evaluate Kubernetes when its primary workflow matches a documented requirement. Run a representative pilot and verify current capabilities, limits and contract terms directly with the vendor.

faqs.question: Are prices and ratings independently verified here?
faqs.answer: No. This review does not present an independently verified price or third-party rating. Check current official documentation and obtain a dated quote.

faqs.question: What should a pilot include?
faqs.answer: Test the main workflow, one failure case, permissions, integrations, export and offboarding. Record pass, partial pass, fail or unknown and assign an owner to every unresolved requirement.

faqs.question: How should total cost be compared?
faqs.answer: Include licenses, usage, implementation, migration, training, integrations, support, internal administration and renewal terms—not only the headline subscription.

author: Marcus Rivera

company.pricingModel: Open source with managed service options

learningCurve: Steep — requires dedicated training time for full proficiency
whoShouldUse: Kubernetes is a possible fit for freelancers who have checked plan limits, invoicing needs, and total cost who need an affordable, easy-to-use developer tools tool. Its simplicity and core feature set make it ideal for solo practitioners.
whoShouldNotUse: Kubernetes may be overwhelming for users who only need basic developer tools functionality. Its extensive feature set can create unnecessary complexity for simple use cases.
